newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM reiterates no baht devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM reiterates no baht devaluation.

text.p: Thailand's Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Sunday reiterated that there would be no devaluation of the baht as still expected by some because of the country's worst economic slump in over a decade.

"We should not discuss currency in public but I can assure you that we will not devalue the baht as the risk will outweigh the initial gain. If we wanted the baht devalued, why would we have defended it the way we did?" he said in an address to the nation on television to mark his six months in office.

Thailand's embattled baht came under foreign speculative attack in mid-May. The central bank successfully defended the currency and punished foreign speculators by cutting off their baht supply from local sources.

The controls have led to a two-tier baht market, one offshore and the other onshore. Despite government assurances, foreign analysts still believe the baht may be devalued or that the government will change the baht system to allow depreciation.
Thailand's economy is in a severe downturn with 1997 growth expected to be the lowest in over a decade at around 5.6 percent against 6.4 percent posted last year.
Exports have turned sluggish, the battered Thai bourse is at its lowest level in eight years and troubles have plagued the ailing finance and depressed property sectors.
Chavalit said he had inherited current problems which had arisen from overspending and borrowing resulting in the twin evils of massive trade and current account deficits.
"The problems of Thailand were that we overborrowed and overspent and financed our spending with foreign debt. That's what we inherited when we took office," he added.
These woes had also affected sentiment in the baht.
"During the past six months we have been in office, we have had to defend the baht twice," he said.
"As a solider I can tell you that sometimes fighting on the battlefield does not cost as much as fighting a battle in the money market," added the premier who once was Thailand's army chief.
Chavalit said he believed the economy was bottoming out. "We have seen the worst and expect to see recovery ahead. Our fundamentals remain good," he added.

He said expansion in exports and investments, the nation's growth engines, had picked up. The modest 1997 export growth target of seven percent was likely to be met. Exports grew by 23 percent in 1995 but contracted 0.2 percent in 1996.

Citing Board of Investment data, Chavalit said in the first five months of this year investments in 411 projects worth around 200 billion baht ($8 billion) had been approved against 405 projects worth 200 billion baht in the same period last year.

On latest measures to force mergers of 16 weak finance companies with stronger ones in the debt-ridden finance sector, he said the move was good as it would weed out the inefficient and unstable firms from the system.
Finance companies are overexposed with billions of baht in non-performing loans to the cash-strapped property sector and their asset quality is highly questionable, analysts said.
Chavalit said the finance sector's woes had been prolonged because in the past there were too many discrepancies between plans to revive the industry and too little action.
"I think we have done the right thing, although financial measures are delicate and depend a lot on their timing," he said.
